etymology: Hebrew Marah, "bitter"; the place in the wilderness where Israel found bitter water that the LORD made sweet by a tree.
biblical_def: Marah was the first stopping-place in the wilderness after Israel crossed the Red Sea, where they found water but could not drink it, "for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah" (Exo 15:23). Three days into the desert with no water, the people murmured against Moses; and Moses cried unto the LORD, "and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet" (Exo 15:25). There God made for them a statute and an ordinance, and proved them, revealing Himself by a new name: "I am the LORD that healeth thee" (Exo 15:26). Marah is one of the richest types in the Old Testament. The bitter waters of a fallen, wilderness world are made sweet only by a tree cast into them — a foreshadowing of the cross of Christ, by which the bitterness of sin, sorrow, and death is transformed into sweetness for the people of God. Marah stands in the dictionary as the place of bitterness made sweet, where God taught Israel that He is the Healer, and where the tree thrown into the bitter waters points to the cross that turns the bitterest providence into a fountain of sweetness for those who trust the LORD.
webster_summary: The wilderness place (Exo 15:23-26) where Israel's bitter water was made sweet by a tree the LORD showed Moses; where God revealed Himself as "the LORD that healeth thee," a type of the cross that turns bitterness to sweetness.

corruption_summary: Marah needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God turns the bitter providences of the wilderness to sweetness by the tree of the cross, and reveals Himself as the Healer of His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Bitterness-without-hope correction. The natural heart, meeting the bitter waters of affliction, murmurs as Israel did and concludes that God has forgotten. Marah teaches otherwise: the same God who led them to the bitter water provided the tree that made it sweet. The dictionary holds that no bitterness in the believer's path is beyond the sweetening power of God; He who showed Moses the tree still casts the cross of Christ into our bitterest providences, and turns the waters sweet.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the typology of the tree. The tree cast into the bitter waters foreshadows the cross, on which Christ was made a curse for us (Gal 3:13), and by which the curse itself is turned to blessing. The dictionary commends the lesson: at Marah God revealed Himself as the Healer, and the wood that healed the waters points to the wood of Calvary, where the bitterness of sin and death is swallowed up in the sweetness of redeeming grace.

etymology: Hebrew Kerith, a brook east of the Jordan where Elijah was hidden and fed by ravens at God's command.
biblical_def: Cherith was a brook east of the Jordan where the prophet Elijah was hidden and miraculously sustained during the great drought he had announced upon apostate Israel. After declaring to King Ahab that there would be neither dew nor rain except by his word, Elijah was commanded by the LORD, "Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kgs 17:3). There God provided for him in a manner both humble and astonishing: "the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook" (1 Kgs 17:6). Ravens, unclean birds known for neglecting their own young, were made the LORD's caterers to His prophet. In time the brook dried up, for there was no rain in the land, and God then sent Elijah on to the widow of Zarephath — teaching the prophet to depend on Him step by step, not on any single means. Cherith stands in the dictionary as the place of God's hidden provision, where the LORD fed His servant by unlikely means in a time of famine, and where the drying of the brook taught Elijah that his trust must rest not in the stream but in the God who commanded it.
webster_summary: A brook east of the Jordan (1 Kgs 17:3-7) where God hid Elijah during the drought and fed him by ravens; when the brook dried up, God sent him on, teaching trust in the Provider rather than the provision.

corruption_summary: Cherith needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is God's faithful provision by unlikely means and the call to trust the Provider rather than any single channel of provision.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-reliance correction. The natural man trusts in his own stores and strategies, not in the unseen care of God. At Cherith Elijah had nothing but the bare promise of the LORD, who fed him by ravens — the most improbable of caterers. The dictionary holds that the heavenly Father who feeds the fowls of the air will surely feed His children (Matt 6:26); the believer is called to rest, like Elijah, in the provision of God, who is never at a loss for means.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is trust in the Provider above the provision. When the brook dried up, Elijah was not abandoned but redirected; God meant him to lean on Himself, not on the stream. The dictionary commends the lesson: the Lord often dries up one means to teach us not to trust in it, and to look past every channel to the God who commands the ravens and the rain alike, and who never fails His own.

etymology: Hebrew Yabboq, a river east of the Jordan; the ford where Jacob wrestled with God and was renamed Israel.
biblical_def: The Jabbok was a river flowing west into the Jordan from the highlands of Gilead, most famous as the scene of Jacob's night of wrestling with God. Returning to meet his brother Esau in great fear, Jacob sent his family and goods across the ford of Jabbok and was left alone; "and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day" (Gen 32:24). The Man — the Angel of the LORD, God Himself in visible form — touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, so that he limped ever after, yet Jacob clung to Him crying, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (Gen 32:26). There God changed his name from Jacob ("supplanter") to Israel, "for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed." Jacob named the place Peniel, "for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved" (Gen 32:30). The Jabbok was also later a boundary of the Ammonites and of the trans-Jordan tribes. It stands in the dictionary as the river of Jacob's transformation, where the supplanter became Israel, where prevailing prayer clung to God and would not let go, and where the man who wrestled God came away both broken and blessed, limping yet a prince.
webster_summary: A river east of the Jordan (Gen 32:22-30) where Jacob wrestled with God all night, was renamed Israel, and named the place Peniel ("I have seen God face to face"); the river of transformation and prevailing prayer.

corruption_paragraphs: Self-sufficiency correction. Jacob the supplanter had schemed and grasped his whole life; at the Jabbok God broke his self-reliance, touching his thigh so he limped ever after. The dictionary holds that God often must wound our self-sufficiency before He can bless us; the prince Israel was made not by Jacob's cunning but by his clinging, and the man who would have power with God must first be broken of his power in himself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is prevailing prayer that will not let go. Jacob clung to God crying, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (Gen 32:26); Hosea says "he wept, and made supplication unto him" (Hos 12:4). The dictionary commends this holy importunity: the believer is invited to wrestle with God in prayer, to cling to His promises, and to refuse to release his hold until the blessing comes — coming away, like Jacob, both humbled and crowned.

etymology: Hebrew Gihon, "gushing"; the spring at Jerusalem where Solomon was anointed king, later channeled into the city by Hezekiah's tunnel.
biblical_def: Gihon was the chief spring supplying water to ancient Jerusalem, in the Kidron valley below the city of David, and the scene of two notable events. First, it was at Gihon that Solomon was anointed king. When Adonijah sought to seize the throne, the aged David commanded that Solomon be set on the royal mule, brought down to Gihon, and there anointed by Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet, with the trumpet blown and the people crying, "God save king Solomon" (1 Kgs 1:38-39). The true heir was crowned at the spring while the usurper feasted nearby. Second, centuries later King Hezekiah, preparing Jerusalem against the Assyrian siege, "stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David" (2 Chr 32:30), cutting the famous tunnel that carried the spring's water safely inside the walls to the pool of Siloam. Gihon stands in the dictionary as the spring of the king's anointing and the city's life, where the rightful son of David was crowned against the pretender, and where a godly king secured the waters of life for the besieged city of God — a quiet emblem of the true Son of David, anointed King, and the living water He gives to His own.
webster_summary: The chief spring of ancient Jerusalem (1 Kgs 1:38; 2 Chr 32:30) where Solomon was anointed king against the usurper Adonijah, and which Hezekiah later channeled into the city by his tunnel against the Assyrian siege.

corruption_summary: Gihon needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the crowning of the rightful Son of David against every pretender, and the provision of living water for the city of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Usurper-versus-heir reading. While Adonijah proclaimed himself king at his own feast, the true heir Solomon was anointed at Gihon by God's appointed priest and prophet. The dictionary sees in this a quiet pattern: the world crowns its own pretenders, but God crowns His chosen King. The usurper's feast ended in fear when the trumpet of the true king sounded; so every rival to the Son of David will fall before the LORD's Anointed, whom God has set upon His holy hill (Psa 2:6).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the living water God gives to His city. Hezekiah's tunnel secured Gihon's waters within the walls against the siege, a picture of God's preservation of His people's life in the day of trouble. The dictionary commends the deeper fulfillment: Christ gives the living water of His Spirit, so that out of the believer's belly flow rivers of living water (John 7:38), a fountain the enemy can never cut off.

etymology: Hebrew Abanah; with Pharpar, one of the two rivers of Damascus that Naaman preferred to the Jordan.
biblical_def: Abana and Pharpar were the two rivers of Damascus, named in the account of Naaman the Syrian, whose pride nearly cost him his healing. Naaman, the great captain of the king of Syria, was a leper; told by a captive Israelite girl of a prophet in Samaria, he came to Elisha, who sent word that he should go and wash in the Jordan seven times and be clean. But Naaman was wroth at so plain a remedy, and at being sent to the muddy Jordan, raging, "Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean?" (2 Kgs 5:12). He turned away in a rage, until his servants reasoned with him: if the prophet had bidden him do some great thing, would he not have done it? How much more this simple word. Humbled, Naaman went down and dipped seven times in Jordan, "and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean" (2 Kgs 5:14). Abana stands in the dictionary as the river of human pride, which would rather wash in its own grand waters than stoop to God's appointed means, and whose lesson is that cleansing comes not by the ways that please our pride but by humble obedience to the simple word of God.

corruption_paragraphs: Pride-of-self correction. Naaman wanted a cure on his own terms, by his own rivers, with some impressive ritual to match his dignity. God's way was humbling: go wash in the despised Jordan. The dictionary holds the abiding lesson against every proud heart: God saves not by the grand and self-flattering ways men prefer, but by the simple, humbling means He appoints; the sinner must stoop to the plain word of the gospel, or perish in his rage like Naaman nearly did.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the offense of God's simple means to human pride. The gospel, like the muddy Jordan, offends those who would rather be saved by some great thing of their own doing. God has chosen the foolish and weak things to confound the wise and mighty (1 Cor 1:27). The dictionary commends Naaman's servants and his eventual obedience: blessed is the proud man who is reasoned down to humble obedience, washes as he is bidden, and comes up clean.

etymology: Hebrew Qishon, a river of the Jezreel valley; the scene of Sisera's defeat and of Elijah's slaughter of the prophets of Baal.
biblical_def: The Kishon was a river draining the valley of Jezreel to the Mediterranean, the scene of two mighty acts of God against His enemies. First, in the days of the judges, when Deborah and Barak went out against Sisera and the chariots of Jabin king of Canaan, the LORD discomfited Sisera; a sudden storm flooded the Kishon, miring his iron chariots, and the song of Deborah exults, "The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon" (Judg 5:21). The waters God had made fought for Israel. Second, after the contest on Mount Carmel, when the fire of the LORD had fallen and the people confessed, "The LORD, he is the God," Elijah commanded that the prophets of Baal be seized, "and brought them down to the brook Kishon, and slew them there" (1 Kgs 18:40), purging the land of the idolatry that had provoked the drought. The Kishon stands in the dictionary as the river of the LORD's judgment on His enemies, where the chariots of the oppressor were swept away and the prophets of a false god were destroyed, a witness that the God of Israel fights for His people and will not leave idolatry unjudged.
webster_summary: A river of the Jezreel valley (Judg 5:21; 1 Kgs 18:40) where the LORD swept away Sisera's chariots in a flood and where Elijah slew the prophets of Baal after Carmel; the river of God's judgment on His enemies.

corruption_summary: Kishon needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the LORD fights for His people and judges idolatry, against a sentimental religion that denies God's righteous judgment on His enemies.
corruption_paragraphs: Judgment-denied correction. A sentimental age recoils from the LORD's judgments at Kishon — the drowned army, the slain prophets — and prefers a God who never opposes evil. Scripture presents the holy God who fights for His oppressed people and will not let idolatry stand. The dictionary holds the righteousness of divine judgment: the same mercy that delivers Israel is the justice that sweeps away her oppressors, and a God who would not judge evil would be no comfort to the afflicted and no terror to the wicked.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD fights for His people. At Kishon the very waters of creation were marshaled against Sisera; the stars in their courses fought against him (Judg 5:20). The dictionary commends the comfort to the faithful: the battles of God's people are the LORD's, and He commands the elements, the armies, and the outcome. Israel had only to obey; the God of Kishon did the fighting.

etymology: Hebrew Besor, a brook in the south of Judah where David established a statute of equal shares for those who guard the supplies.
biblical_def: Besor was a brook in the far south of Judah, near Ziklag, the scene of one of David's most gracious rulings. When the Amalekites had raided Ziklag and carried off the wives and children of David and his men, David pursued with six hundred men; but at the brook Besor, two hundred were "so faint that they could not go over," and stayed behind with the baggage (1 Sam 30:9-10). With the remaining four hundred David overtook the Amalekites and recovered all. When they returned, certain "wicked men and men of Belial" among the four hundred said the two hundred who had stayed should receive none of the spoil except their own wives and children. But David refused: "ye shall not do so, my brethren, with that which the LORD hath given us... but as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff: they shall part alike" (1 Sam 30:23-24). And he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel from that day forward. Besor stands in the dictionary as the brook of equal shares, where David taught that the victory and its spoil are the LORD's gift, and that those who keep the supplies share alike with those who fight — a principle of grace that honors every faithful servant in the Lord's work, seen and unseen.
webster_summary: A brook in southern Judah (1 Sam 30:9-24) where David's two hundred faint men stayed with the supplies; on returning victorious, David ruled that they who guard the baggage share the spoil equally with those who fight, and made it a statute in Israel.

corruption_summary: Besor needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the LORD's victory is His gift to be shared, and that those who serve unseen, guarding the supplies, are honored equally with those who fight.
corruption_paragraphs: Merit-only correction. The wicked men at Besor reckoned reward strictly by visible exertion: only those who fought should share the spoil. David reckoned by grace: the victory was the LORD's gift, not their achievement, and all who served, seen and unseen, should share alike. The dictionary holds the principle against a merit-obsessed spirit: in the Lord's work the reward rests on His grace, and the humble servant who keeps the supplies is not forgotten before God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honor of unseen service. Those who tarry by the stuff — who pray, who give, who labor in hidden and unglamorous ways — share in the victory with those on the front lines. The dictionary commends David's statute: as the members that seem more feeble are necessary (1 Cor 12:22), so the Lord values every faithful servant in His cause, and will reward the hidden labor as surely as the visible.

etymology: Hebrew Merom, the waters in northern Canaan where Joshua defeated the great coalition of northern kings.
biblical_def: The waters of Merom were a lake or marsh in the highlands of northern Canaan, the scene of Joshua's climactic victory over the last great Canaanite coalition. When Jabin king of Hazor heard of Israel's conquests, he summoned the kings of the north, who gathered with their armies, horses, and chariots "even as the sand that is upon the sea shore in multitude... to fight against Israel" and "pitched together at the waters of Merom" (Josh 11:4-5). The LORD encouraged Joshua, "Be not afraid because of them: for to morrow about this time will I deliver them up all slain before Israel" (Josh 11:6). Joshua fell upon them suddenly at the waters of Merom and smote them, chasing them to the gates of great Sidon; in obedience to God's command, he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire, refusing to trust in the very weapons the world relied on. With this victory the back of Canaanite resistance was broken, and Joshua took the whole land. The waters of Merom stand in the dictionary as the place of the last great conquest, where God delivered an innumerable host with its horses and chariots into Israel's hand, and where Joshua, by burning the chariots, taught that Israel's strength was in the LORD, not in the armaments of the nations.
webster_summary: A lake in northern Canaan (Josh 11:5-7) where Joshua defeated the great coalition of northern kings with their horses and chariots; in obedience he hamstrung the horses and burned the chariots, breaking Canaanite resistance.

corruption_summary: Merom needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God delivers the innumerable hosts of the world into His people's hand, and that Israel's strength is in the LORD, not in horses and chariots.
corruption_paragraphs: Strength-in-arms correction. The northern kings trusted in their multitude and their iron chariots; Israel was commanded to burn those very chariots and hamstring the horses, refusing to adopt the world's confidence. The dictionary holds the lesson of Psalm 20:7: "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God." God's people are not to lean on the arm of flesh or the armaments of the nations, but on the LORD who gives the victory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is courage grounded in God's promise. Faced with a host like the sand of the sea, Joshua was told, "Be not afraid." The dictionary commends the pattern: the size of the enemy is nothing against the word of God, who had already decreed the outcome. The believer facing overwhelming odds may take the same comfort — the battle is the LORD's, and His promise, not the enemy's strength, decides the day.

etymology: Hebrew Kebar, a river or canal in Babylonia where Ezekiel, among the exiles, received his visions of God.
biblical_def: The Chebar was a great river or canal in the land of the Chaldeans, by which the prophet Ezekiel dwelt among the Jewish exiles, and where he received his overwhelming visions of God. "Now it came to pass... as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God" (Ezek 1:1). There, far from the temple and the holy land, by the waters of a foreign and pagan country, the glory of the LORD appeared to Ezekiel in the vision of the four living creatures, the wheels, and the throne-chariot, with One above it in the appearance of a man surrounded with the brightness of the rainbow — "the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD" (Ezek 1:28). By the Chebar Ezekiel was called and commissioned as a watchman to the house of Israel. The vision taught the captives a truth they sorely needed: that the glory of God was not confined to Jerusalem, but had come to His people even in Babylon, and that the sovereign LORD reigned on His throne over all the earth. The Chebar stands in the dictionary as the river of Ezekiel's visions, where God met His exiled people in a strange land, and proved that no captivity can shut His glory out, nor any distance separate His own from the presence of their God.
webster_summary: A river or canal in Babylonia (Ezek 1:1-3) where Ezekiel, among the exiles, saw his visions of God's throne-chariot and glory; proof that God's presence was not confined to Jerusalem but came to His people even in captivity.

corruption_summary: Chebar needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God's presence and glory reach His people even in exile, and that no captivity can confine the reign of the sovereign LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: God-confined correction. The exiles might have supposed that God's glory was bound to the temple in Jerusalem, and that in Babylon they were cut off from Him. By the Chebar God shattered that despair, bringing the vision of His throne-chariot — mobile, sovereign, unconfined — to His captive people. The dictionary holds that the LORD is not localized or limited; His glory met the exiles by a pagan river, and He is present with His people wherever they are scattered, for the whole earth is full of His glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the powers of the world. The throne-chariot vision revealed the LORD reigning above the wheels and the living creatures, governing all things even from the midst of Babylon. The dictionary commends the comfort to a scattered and pressured church: though God's people sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep (Psa 137:1), their God reigns over Babylon itself, and His glory has not abandoned them.

etymology: Hebrew Arnon, a river and gorge east of the Dead Sea forming the border of Moab.
biblical_def: The Arnon was a river running through a deep gorge into the eastern side of the Dead Sea, forming the historic boundary of Moab. As Israel journeyed toward the promised land, the Arnon marked the frontier between Moab to the south and the Amorite kingdom of Sihon to the north: "For Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites" (Num 21:13). Israel, forbidden to attack Moab, passed by and then requested peaceful passage through Sihon's land; when Sihon refused and came out to war, the LORD delivered him into Israel's hand, and they possessed his land from the Arnon northward (Num 21:24). The Arnon thus became the southern boundary of the trans-Jordan inheritance given to Reuben. The river is remembered in the Book of the Wars of the LORD and in Israel's later disputes with Moab, when Jephthah recounted this history to the king of Ammon (Judg 11:18-26). The Arnon stands in the dictionary as a boundary-river of the inheritance, a witness to the LORD's faithful gift of the land to His people according to His promise, and to His ordering of the nations and their borders, that He might bring Israel into the place He had appointed for them.

corruption_summary: Arnon needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the LORD's faithful gift of the inheritance and His sovereign ordering of the nations and their borders.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithfulness of God in giving His people their inheritance. At the Arnon, Israel stood on the threshold of possessing the land God had promised to Abraham centuries before. The dictionary holds that God keeps His covenant promises across generations; the boundary-river marks not merely a line of geography but a milestone of fulfilled promise, as the LORD brought His people, step by appointed step, into the land of their inheritance.

God's-ordering-of-nations note. Scripture records that God Himself appointed the borders of the nations — giving Moab and Ammon their lands, which Israel was forbidden to seize, and delivering Sihon's land to Israel. The dictionary holds that the LORD has determined the times and bounds of the peoples' habitation (Acts 17:26); the Arnon, dividing Moab from the Amorites and marking Israel's inheritance, witnesses to the God who sets the boundaries of nations according to His sovereign will and faithful promise.
